title: Product Count And Average Price Per Band
outcome: 🆕 new practice question — not attempted yet
watchOutFor: Group by the same CASE expression (or its alias / ordinal), not by `unit_price`.
problem: Following the price-band labels, pricing wants a summary: how many products fall into each band and their price range.
objective: For each price band (Budget < 20, Mid-range < 50, Premium), return the product count, min, max and average price.
expectedOutput:
| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| price_band | Budget / Mid-range / Premium |
| product_count | Number of products |
| min_price | Lowest price in band |
| max_price | Highest price in band |
| avg_price | Average price, 2 dp |

| price_band | product_count | min_price | max_price | avg_price |
|------------|---------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| Budget | 39 | 2.50 | 19.50 | 13.02 |
| Mid-range | 31 | 20.00 | 49.30 | 31.59 |
| Premium | 7 | 53.00 | 263.50 | 105.11 |

*(Sample rows are illustrative — the first few rows from the practice dataset, shown to convey shape/format; your data instance may differ.)*
approach:
1. Compute the band with `CASE`.
2. `GROUP BY` the band alias.
3. Aggregate `COUNT`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `AVG`.
4. Order by `min_price` so bands appear cheapest first.
mySolution:
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN unit_price < 20 THEN 'Budget'
        WHEN unit_price < 50 THEN 'Mid-range'
        ELSE 'Premium'
    END AS price_band,
    COUNT(*)                  AS product_count,
    MIN(unit_price)           AS min_price,
    MAX(unit_price)           AS max_price,
    ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY price_band
ORDER BY min_price;

referenceQuery:
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN unit_price < 20 THEN 'Budget'
        WHEN unit_price < 50 THEN 'Mid-range'
        ELSE 'Premium'
    END AS price_band,
    COUNT(*)                  AS product_count,
    MIN(unit_price)           AS min_price,
    MAX(unit_price)           AS max_price,
    ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY price_band
ORDER BY min_price;
why: PostgreSQL allows `GROUP BY` an output-column alias, so the `CASE` is written once. Each row is bucketed first, then the aggregates run per bucket. The bands do not overlap, so `min_price` is unique per band and gives a natural low-to-high order.
pitfalls: Grouping by `unit_price` — you get one row per price, not per band.
Ordering by `price_band` alphabetically: Budget, Mid-range, Premium happens to work here, but generally it will not.
Using an alias in `WHERE`/`HAVING` — not allowed; repeat the expression or wrap in a subquery.

followups.question: Is `GROUP BY alias` standard SQL?
followups.answer: No — it is a PostgreSQL/MySQL extension. Portable code repeats the `CASE` or groups in a derived table.

followups.question: How would you include bands with zero products?
followups.answer: Generate the bands from a `VALUES` list and `LEFT JOIN` the products onto it.

followups.question: How would you get the share of products per band?

takeaway: Bucket with `CASE`, group by the bucket, then aggregate — the CASE becomes the grouping key.
